def count_shelf_orders(counts, k):
    """
    Count the arrangements of a multiset of colored volumes in a row that
    have EXACTLY k adjacent same-color pairs.

    You are given `counts`, a list of m positive integers: counts[i] is the
    number of volumes of color i. Volumes of the same color are
    indistinguishable from each other; volumes of different colors are
    distinguishable. All S = sum(counts) volumes are placed in a single row.
    For an arrangement w[0], ..., w[S-1] (where w[p] is the color at
    position p), an *adjacent pair* is an index p with 0 <= p <= S-2 and
    w[p] == w[p+1]. Two arrangements are distinct iff their color sequences
    differ.

    Return the exact number of distinct arrangements whose number of
    adjacent pairs equals k, as a Python int (exact arbitrary-precision
    arithmetic; the answer can exceed 10**250, so floating point is useless).

    Input domain (the function must be correct and fast on all of it):
      * 1 <= m = len(counts) <= 30
      * every counts[i] is an int with counts[i] >= 1
      * S = sum(counts) <= 200
      * k is an int with 0 <= k <= 250 (note k may exceed S)

    Behavior details: if S == 1 the single arrangement has 0 adjacent
    pairs, so the answer is 1 iff k == 0; the maximum attainable number of
    adjacent pairs is S - m (each color in one solid block), so any
    k > S - m must return 0. The order of colors in `counts` does not
    affect the answer. There is no tie-breaking: the output is one exact
    integer count. Enumeration of arrangements is hopeless at S = 200; the
    intended solution counts combinatorially.

    >>> count_shelf_orders([2, 1], 1)
    2
    >>> count_shelf_orders([2, 2], 0)
    2
    >>> count_shelf_orders([3, 2, 2], 2)
    62
    """
